title: The coiled one remains
hook: what if four children were killed; the coiled serpent still lives, he writes (Zafarnama)

segments.voice: Yesterday, broken oaths: an emperor held to the promises he made in God's name. Your line was keep your oath.

Some sentences are short because nothing more could be said. The Zafarnama has one of those. Sikh tradition remembers what came before the letter: the Guru's four sons were killed. Two, tradition says, fell fighting. Two, still small boys, were put to death because they would not give up their faith. You heard their story on days eighty-nine and ninety. A father who had lost all four children wrote to the emperor, and the line he wrote about it is not a lament. It's a question, followed by an image Sikhs still repeat.
screen: `A SHORT SENTENCE.` → `FOUR SONS LOST.` → `A QUESTION, THEN AN IMAGE.`

segments.voice: Paraphrased, the line runs like this: what of it, if you have killed four children? The coiled serpent still remains. The first half names the worst thing that could happen to a parent, and names it flatly, almost as a shrug. That flatness is not coldness. It's refusal. He will not let the loss be the end of the sentence. The second half turns to the coiled one. A coiled snake is a snake at rest and fully alive, gathered into itself, not beaten. Readers hear different things in it. Some hear the Guru speaking of himself: you took my sons, and I am still here. Some hear the Khalsa, the community he had formed: you can kill children, and you have not killed the people. Some hear both, and a warning folded inside: a coiled thing can still rise. Whichever reading, the line is about what remains after the loss, not about the loss itself. And stay with what it doesn't say. It doesn't say the grief is small. Sikhs remember the four sons, the Sahibzade, with deep sorrow, in the Ardas and at gatherings that mark their deaths. The coiled one remains is not a way of skipping the mourning. It's what stands up in the middle of it.
screen: `WHAT OF IT, IF YOU KILLED FOUR CHILDREN?` · `A COILED SERPENT: AT REST, ALIVE.` · `THE GURU, THE KHALSA, OR BOTH?` · `NOT SKIPPING THE MOURNING.` · then, large: `STILL STANDING.`

segments.voice: If it feels right, bring to mind a loss you've carried and let it be as heavy as it is; then, gently, look for what is still standing in you: a habit you kept, someone you still look after, a way you still laugh. If you pray, hold both the loss and what remains in Waheguru. If a loss ever feels heavier than you can carry, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
The coiled one remains. In the Zafarnama, after naming the killing of his four sons, Guru Gobind Singh writes that the coiled serpent still lives. Today's word.
Your line: still standing. Coiled and quiet is not the same as beaten. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember the four Sahibzade in the Ardas and at gatherings that mark their martyrdom; the Zafarnama's line about the coiled serpent is often recited in katha and at those gatherings.

chat.says: How could a father say 'what of it' about losing four children? Was he cold?
options: No. It's refusal: he won't let the loss end the sentence, and the grief stays real.
Yes. He was saying his sons' deaths didn't really matter very much to him.
No. He wrote it before anyone had told him that his sons had been killed.
chat.meaning: The flatness isn't coldness; it's refusal. Sikhs mourn the four sons with deep sorrow, and the coiled one remains is what stands up in the middle of it.

Zafarnama.meaning: the Guru's letter in Persian verse to the emperor

Sahibzade.meaning: the Guru's four sons, remembered with deep love

Khalsa.meaning: the community of initiated Sikhs the tenth Guru formed

sources.ref: Zafarnama (Dasam Granth), the verse on the four children and the coiled serpent

notes: Both Zafarnama verses are paraphrased; please check the paraphrase ('what of it, if you have killed four children? the coiled serpent still remains') and that the sparks/fire image sits nearby.
The deaths of the four Sahibzade (two in battle, two put to death as small boys for refusing to give up their faith) are given as tradition; names, places and ages are deliberately left out.
The three readings of the coiled serpent (the Guru, the Khalsa, both) are offered as what readers hear; please confirm they are fair.
'Gather each winter to mark their deaths' refers to the Shaheedi commemorations in December (Poh); please confirm the wording.
